title: FORT-Searcher: Shortcut-Resistant Tasks for Search Agents
hook: Harder-looking questions aren't harder to search. FORT builds tasks where the intended search can't collapse into a cheap shortcut — and trains better deep-search agents on them.
key_points: Training search agents needs questions whose answers stay hidden until enough evidence is gathered — but structural complexity alone doesn't guarantee that.
The intended multi-step search can collapse via a cheaper identifying route; FORT names four shortcut risks.
Those risks: evidence co-coverage, single-clue selectivity, exposed constants, and prior-knowledge binding.

FORT diagnoses realized difficulty with trajectory signatures (solving cost, answer-hit time, prior-shortcut rate) and controls risk across entity selection, graph construction, question formulation, and adversarial refinement.
Training on the resulting trajectories with SFT only yields the best overall performance among comparable open-source search agents.
content_html: Training a "deep search" agent needs verifiable questions whose answers stay out of reach until the agent has actually searched and gathered enough evidence. A common way to make tasks look harder is to enrich the underlying graph structure — but the authors point out that structural complexity alone doesn't guarantee realized search difficulty: the intended search process can quietly collapse through a cheaper identifying route, a shortcut.
extra_html: They formalize this with a shortcut-aware difficulty framework and name four actionable shortcut risks — evidence co-coverage, single-clue selectivity, exposed constants, and prior-knowledge binding — and diagnose their effects with trajectory signatures like solving cost, answer-hit time, and prior-shortcut rate. FORT (a Framework of shOrtcut-Resistant Training-data synthesis) then controls those risks across entity selection, evidence-graph construction, question formulation, and adversarial refinement. The synthesized data induces longer pre-answer search and fewer shortcut patterns than existing open datasets; training FORT-Searcher on those trajectories with supervised fine-tuning alone gives the best overall results among comparable-size open-source search agents. The transferable lesson is about data quality: when synthesizing training tasks, design against the cheap path, not just for surface difficulty.

related.title: Harness-1: RL for Search Agents with State-Externalizing Harnesses
related.hook: Stop making the policy remember everything. Harness-1 moves a search agent's bookkeeping into the environment, so RL only has to learn the decisions that matter.

related.title: Self-Instruct: Aligning LMs with Self-Generated Instructions
related.hook: Instead of paying humans to write instruction data, have the model write its own — bootstrap instructions, inputs, and outputs from its own generations, filter, and fine-tune.

flashcards.prompt: Why isn't a structurally complex question necessarily a hard search task?
flashcards.back_html: The intended multi-step search can collapse through a cheaper identifying route — a shortcut — so apparent (structural) difficulty doesn't guarantee realized search difficulty.

flashcards.prompt: What does FORT do to make training tasks 'shortcut-resistant'?

choices.text: Controls shortcut risks across entity selection, evidence-graph construction, question formulation, and adversarial refinement
Adds more entities to the underlying knowledge graph
Shortens the questions to reduce ambiguity

flashcards.explanation_html: FORT targets shortcut risks at each construction stage so the answer can't be reached cheaply, forcing a genuine multi-step search.

flashcards.prompt: Name one of FORT's four shortcut risks.
flashcards.back_html: Any of: evidence co-coverage, single-clue selectivity, exposed constants, or prior-knowledge binding.
